title: Long engagements: the Halfway House and the Metairie Inn
summary: He recalls house bands and his nine years at the Halfway House with Abbie Brunies.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Well he played with, uh, he played with Rhythm Kings, like I told ya. And they had a band for years. They played at the, at the, the first little club. You see there was two little clubs there. The first one was right on the corner of Dryads and Common. Well they had a band in there with, uh, fiddle, bass, piano, and drums. And, uh, Johnny Beisdorff's brother, a cousin, I don't know whether his brother is, I think it's his cousin. Leonard Beisdorff. He was another black, black key piano player. He played piano. And, and Oscar played fiddle. And, uh, they had the little Angelo Parmesan on, on Badger and Chink. And they worked there for, I don't know how many years. Cause in those days Dick, you didn't, you didn't stay last maybe four, five weeks, six weeks. You stayed, I like that, I worked nine years at the halfway house. See, just the halfway house alone. And then, I worked with Abbie at the, at the, at the Metri Inn. For about three years. That was a gambling house. And I worked with him at the Silver Slipper for about three years. Well, no, if you had a good band, you went on a job, you stayed there for, indefinitely, you know. For years and years. Just like that, that P-Rod, he must have been twenty years out there at the, what's it called? Spanish Fort.

And, uh, the halfway house, the Burnts was a tradition out there. It couldn't be the halfway house without, I think, I, I don't think there's anybody else ever played in there. But Abbie. I think after, after Abbie left, they closed up. Made an ice cream pallet out of it.
